client: I've been having a really hard time since my mom passed away from cancer last year. I keep trying to push through at work, but I'll be sitting at my desk and suddenly I just can't concentrate on anything — it's like my mind goes completely blank or I start thinking about her and lose an hour. I'm not sure talking about it is actually going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try something because I can't keep going on like this.
therapist: Thank you for taking this step — it takes real courage to reach out, especially when part of you isn't sure it will help. Losing your mom to cancer is one of the most profound losses a person can carry, and what you're describing at work — that sudden blankness, those hours lost in memory — sounds like grief finding its way through even when you're trying to hold it at bay. I'd really like to understand more about what this has been like for you; can you tell me a little about what those moments feel like when your mind drifts to her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: It's hard to describe exactly, but it usually starts with something small — like I'll see a sticky note in her handwriting that I kept, or someone at work will mention their mom offhand, and then it's like I get pulled under. I end up replaying the last few weeks in the hospital, wondering if I did enough, if I was there enough, and then I just feel this heavy guilt sitting on my chest. By the time I snap back to reality, I've missed half a meeting or forgotten what I was even supposed to be doing.
therapist: That image of being "pulled under" by something as small as a sticky note really captures how grief can ambush us in the most ordinary moments — your nervous system is still so attuned to her. The guilt you're describing, that wondering if you did enough, is incredibly common in grief, but I want to gently ask: when you replay those last weeks, what does the evidence actually tell you about the kind of presence you were for her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I mean, logically I know I took time off work to be there, I drove her to appointments, I stayed overnight at the hospital more than once. But when I'm in those moments, logic doesn't really seem to matter — my brain just goes straight to the one afternoon I left early because I had a work deadline, and it makes that feel like the whole story. I guess I hear what you're saying, but it's hard to believe the evidence when the guilt feels so much louder than the facts.
therapist: What you just described is actually a really important insight — you can see the pattern happening, that your mind is cherry-picking that one afternoon and treating it as the whole truth, even while you're living it. In CBT we call this a thinking trap, where one painful memory drowns out a much larger body of evidence — the drives, the overnight stays, the time you gave her. I'm curious: if a close friend described doing everything you did for their mother, and then felt consumed by guilt over leaving once for a work deadline, what would you say to them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I know I'd tell a friend that they did more than enough, that one afternoon doesn't erase everything else they gave. But when I try to turn that around on myself it just feels hollow, like I'm saying the words without actually believing them — there's this voice that says I'm just letting myself off the hook too easily. I'm not sure how you're supposed to actually feel the truth of something instead of just intellectually knowing it.
therapist: That gap between knowing something and truly *feeling* it is one of the most frustrating parts of grief, and the fact that your voice is carrying so much more pain than your words alone suggest tells me this runs really deep for you. That inner voice calling it "letting yourself off the hook" is worth paying attention to — it sounds less like a fair judge and more like a guard that's been protecting you from something. I wonder, what do you think it would mean for you to actually believe you were enough — is there something that feels unsafe or even disloyal about letting that guilt go?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That question actually stopped me for a second, because I think there might be something to it — like if I stop feeling guilty, it's almost like I'm closing a door on her, or admitting that it's really over and she's really gone. The guilt at least keeps me connected to her in some way, even if it's painful. I'm not sure I'm ready to examine that too closely, honestly, because it feels like it could open up something even bigger than the guilt itself.
therapist: What you just uncovered is profound — that the guilt isn't just guilt, it's a way of staying close to her, of keeping the relationship alive in the only way that still feels available to you. And I notice as you said it, there was something in how you spoke that felt like you were moving quickly past something that clearly landed hard, like part of you wanted to say it before another part could stop you. That "something bigger" you're sensing underneath — you don't have to rush toward it, but I want you to know that grief and love can coexist without guilt needing to be the bridge; would you be open to exploring, slowly, what staying connected to her might look like that doesn't cost you so much pain?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I want to say yes, but I'm also sitting here thinking — what would that even look like, staying connected to her without the guilt? Like, the guilt is so woven into how I think about her right now that I can't really picture what's left if I take it away. I guess I'm open to trying, but I'm a little scared it might just feel empty, like I'd lose even that painful connection and end up with nothing.
therapist: The fear that removing the guilt might leave emptiness makes complete sense, but I'd gently offer this: the guilt isn't actually *her* — your love for her, your memories, the sticky note in her handwriting, those belong to a different part of you that guilt has been overshadowing. What if we started very small, not by taking anything away, but just by noticing one moment where you feel connected to her through something other than pain — a memory that brings a flicker of warmth, or something she gave you that makes you smile? That wouldn't be losing her; it might actually be a way of finding more of her.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: There's actually one memory that came to mind just now without me even trying — she used to make this terrible, overly sweet tea that nobody else liked, and she'd always act offended when I made a face at it, and it makes me want to smile even just thinking about it. But then almost immediately I felt guilty for smiling, like that's not allowed somehow. I guess I see what you're pointing at, but I'm not sure I trust myself to sit with the warm memories without the guilt rushing in to cancel them out.
therapist: That memory of the terrible sweet tea is *exactly* the kind of thing I was hoping you might find — it's so specific and so *her*, and the smile it brought is not a betrayal, it's actually love in its purest form. The guilt rushing in to cancel that warmth is the pattern we want to gently work with over time, because smiling at who she was keeps her far more alive than punishing yourself ever could. Would you be willing, just as a small experiment, to let that smile stay for a moment longer next time — not to push the guilt away, but just to see if both things can exist at once?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think I can try that, but I'm already anticipating that the guilt is going to feel louder than the smile and I'll end up just feeling worse for having tried. It's like I don't fully trust my own ability to hold both things at once without one swallowing the other. I guess the honest question is — what do I actually do in that moment when the guilt does rush in, because I don't want to just be left sitting there with it and no idea what to do next?
therapist: That's exactly the right question to ask, and it shows real self-awareness that you're thinking ahead rather than just hoping for the best. When the guilt rushes in, try this: notice it, name it gently to yourself — "there's the guilt" — without fighting it or following it down the spiral, and then see if you can place one hand on that sweet tea memory at the same time, not instead of the guilt, but alongside it. You don't have to resolve the tension or make the guilt disappear; you're just practicing the idea that there's enough room in you for both, and that the smile doesn't have to ask the guilt's permission to exist.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That phrase — "the smile doesn't have to ask the guilt's permission" — actually hit me in a way I wasn't expecting, and I'm sitting with it for a second. I think I can try the noticing and naming part, that feels manageable, but I'm worried that in the actual moment when I'm at my desk and it hits me, I'll forget all of this and just get swept away like I always do. Is it normal to feel like the gap between understanding something in a calm conversation and actually doing it when you're emotional is just enormous?
therapist: That gap you're describing is not only normal, it's one of the most universal experiences in this kind of work — understanding something in a quiet moment and accessing it in the storm are genuinely different skills, and the second one takes practice, not just insight. So rather than trying to remember everything we talked about, what if you gave yourself just one anchor — even something as simple as the words "sweet tea" — that could interrupt the spiral for a single breath and remind you that there's another way to be with her. Over time, that pause gets a little longer, and that's where the change actually lives.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: "Sweet tea" — I actually like that, it's simple enough that I think I could remember it even when I'm not okay. I'm still a little skeptical that one word is going to be enough to pull me back when I'm really in the middle of it, but I think it's worth trying because it's at least connected to something real about her rather than just some technique I'm supposed to remember. I guess I'm cautiously willing to try it this week and see what happens.
therapist: "Cautiously willing" is actually a beautiful place to be — it's honest, and it means you're not forcing yourself to believe something before you've had a chance to test it. The fact that "sweet tea" works for you *because* it's real, because it's her, tells me your instincts about your own healing are already pretty good. I'll be curious to hear what happens this week — not whether it worked perfectly, but just what you noticed.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
